2026 International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations: Summary from the Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid Task Forces.
abstract: This is the annual summary of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations; a comprehensive review was completed in 2025. This latest summary addresses the most recent published resuscitation evidence reviewed by International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation task forces, including Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid. Members from these 6 task forces assessed the certainty of the evidence using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria, and their statements include consensus treatment recommendations. Highlights from task force discussions and insights into how decisions regarding treatment recommendations were made are provided in the Justification and Evidence-to-Decision Framework Highlights sections. The task forces also listed priority knowledge gaps for further research.

Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting - A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) treats hemodynamically unstable bradycardia refractory to pharmacologic management. Effective TCP requires electrical and mechanical capture to augment perfusion. Little is known about prehospital TCP and capture incidence.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients treated with prehospital TCP by an emergency medical services agency between 2017 and 2024. Continuous ECG recordings from cardiac monitors were reviewed. Electrical capture was the primary outcome, defined as a widened QRS with a distinct T wave following a TCP spike. Secondary measures included capture duration, clinician-verbalized pulse during pacing, plethysmograph waveform alignment, and changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse oximetry, and end-tidal carbon dioxide.
RESULTS: Fifty-six patients received attempted TCP. Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR] 58-85), and 34% were female. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered in 59% of patients. Electrical capture was achieved in 18 patients (32%). Among patients who achieved electrical capture, complete capture occurred a mean of 27.2% (standard deviation 30.5%) of attempted pacing duration. The median SBP change was +22.0 (IQR: -2-82) mmHg in patients with electrical capture and 0.0 (IQR: -29-7) mmHg in those with only rare-to-absent capture (p = 0.031). During TCP, clinicians verbalized a palpable pulse 26 times across 19 patients. Only 4 instances (15%) coincided with electrical capture.
CONCLUSIONS: Electrical capture during prehospital TCP occurred in a minority of patients and was often intermittent. Prehospital identification of mechanical capture using routine clinical indicators was difficult and unreliable. Future work should standardize capture definitions and physiologic measurements to determine when TCP produces clinically meaningful perfusion.

title: The Accuracy and Precision of Gravity-Driven Infusions.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: When infusion pumps are unavailable in the prehospital setting, clinicians must estimate fluid flow by counting drops in a drip chamber. We aimed to assess the accuracy and precision of gravity-driven infusions and to estimate the magnitude of inaccuracy and imprecision attributable to human and non-human factors.
METHODS: We recruited 55 paramedics to participate in structured, experimental, simulated study under controlled laboratory conditions, in which each participant set nine drip rates as accurately as possible on a standardized setup. Measurements of flow were made visually (drip rate) and volumetrically (delivered fluid). Volumetric measurements were used to represent overall error, visual measurements were used to represent human error, and the difference was used to represent non-human error. We measured accuracy (percentage error) and precision (mean absolute deviation) using the natural log of error factor to represent the multiplicative decomposition of human and non-human error additively. Mixed effect models were used to assess accuracy and precision across targeted drip rates.
RESULTS: Inaccuracy and imprecision varied by targeted drip rate. Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% (95%CI, -52.7% to -36.8%) to 5.8% (95%CI, -8.5% to 22.3%). Human inaccuracy ranged from -38.8% (95%CI, -46.0% to -30.8%) to 44.1% (95%CI, 27.1% to 63.4%). Non-human inaccuracy ranged from -26.7% (95%CI, -30.1% to -23.2%) to -6.8% (95%CI -11.1% to -2.3%). Imprecision was primarily driven by human factors. The degree of human variation between trial participants ranged from 24.2% (95%CI, 15.3% to 33.7%) to 43.7% (95%CI, 33.4% to 54.9%) across targeted rates. The targeted drip rate of 1gtt/s was more accurate than the pool of all other targeted rates (absolute error 31.1% versus 48.5%). Targeted drip rates of whole numbers were more accurate than targeted drip rates of fractional numbers (absolute error 40.7% versus 54.1%). Targeted drip rates below 1gtt/s were more accurate than rates above 1gtt/s (absolute error 35.3% versus 63.1%).
CONCLUSIONS: Gravity-driven fluid delivery exhibits inaccuracy and imprecision, which varies by targeted rate. While potentially modifiable human factors may improve the accuracy of this technique, non-human error contributes substantially to inaccuracy. There is a need to assess whether this inaccuracy and imprecision adversely affect patient outcomes.

title: Wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: A systematic review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with survival strongly dependent on rapid recognition and timely emergency care. Wearables capable of automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting may reduce delays to treatment, particularly in unwitnessed arrests.Therefore, this review aims to systematically evaluate the existing evidence on the performance of wearable sensors and algorithms designed for OHCA detection.
METHODS: A systematic search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Libraries, forward citation and backward citation to identify all eligible studies up to 22 September 2026. Studies describing non-invasive, intended wearable systems designed to detect OHCA and reporting on their detection performance were included. The methodology and report of the present review are based on recommendations of the PRISMA statement and Cochrane Collaboration. Primary outcome is the sensitivity for cardiac arrest detection. Secondary outcomes include false positives cardiac arrest alerts and specificity. Studies were evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool.
RESULTS: From 6,344 records screened, 13 publications were included with the number of participants ranging from 18 to 1,423. Wristbands were the most prevalent device type (n=9). Nine studies used photoplethysmography as primary sensor type, with accelerometry as additive sensor modality (n=2). Other sensors used were mechanical plethysmography (n=1), electrocardiography (n=1), sound-based (n=1) and a nonlinear resonant circuit (n=1). Sensitivity ranged between 43.8 and 100%, with ten studies reporting a sensitivity of ≥ 90%. False positives ranged between multiple per day and one per twenty-one user-years.
DISCUSSION: Wearable devices have demonstrated promising sensitivity for detecting cardiac arrest. However, (external) validation and real-life data are scarce, and the sensitivity-false alarm trade-off requires further investigation.
REGISTRATION: OSF, doi: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AEPF8.

title: Long-Term Survival Following Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Two-Center Five-Year Analysis.
abstract: Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4%-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years to 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

title: Post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation and coronary angiographic phenotypes in angiography-evaluable survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The clinical meaning of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with suspected coronary etiology remains uncertain. We aimed to describe coronary angiographic phenotypes and clinical outcomes according to post-resuscitation ST-segment findings in an angiography-evaluable subset of OHCA survivors with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 149 successfully resuscitated OHCA patients admitted to our institution between January 2015 and December 2023, who underwent post-resuscitation coronary angiography and had presumed culprit lesions, defined by integrating angiographic findings with electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and biomarker data in the clinical context. Patients were classified according to the presence or absence of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation.
RESULTS: ST-segment elevation was associated with a more acute occlusive coronary phenotype, with more impaired culprit-vessel flow and greater myocardial injury. In contrast, patients without ST-segment elevation more frequently had multivessel disease and chronic total occlusion, suggesting more complex coronary artery disease. Favorable neurological outcome was less frequent with ST-segment elevation in unadjusted analyses, but this association was not independent of pre-hospital factors.
CONCLUSIONS: In this selected OHCA subset, post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation was associated with an acute occlusive coronary phenotype and greater myocardial injury, as in non-arrest acute coronary syndromes. However, the absence of ST-segment elevation did not exclude a coronary culprit lesion, so comprehensive coronary assessment is essential. ST-segment elevation was not independently associated with clinical outcomes after adjustment for pre-hospital factors. These findings should be interpreted considering substantial selection inherent to the study population.

Decreased early bystander CPR initiation despite stable overall rates: a nationwide time-to-event analysis during the COVID-19 pandemic.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Timely bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BCPR) is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). While overall BCPR rates during the COVID-19 pandemic have been inconsistently reported, BCPR initiation timing has received limited attention. This study assessed BCPR initiation within 10 min after witnessed OHCA.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used the All-Japan Utstein registry. Adults with non-traumatic, layperson-witnessed OHCA during March 11-December 31 of 2019 and 2020 were included. The primary outcome was BCPR initiation within 10 min after witnessing. Kaplan-Meier and Cox models were used for time-to-event analyses. Exploratory logistic regression examined associations between BCPR timing and 1-month outcomes.
RESULTS: Among 56,082 eligible cases (27,770 pre-pandemic; 28,312 pandemic), overall BCPR rates were stable (58.7% vs. 58.6%, p = 0.759). However, time-to-event analysis detected a modest difference in early BCPR initiation (log-rank p = 0.010), with a lower hazard during the pandemic (aHR 0.96; 95% CI 0.93-0.98). Among BCPR recipients, earlier initiation was associated with higher odds of a favorable neurological outcome at 1 month (aORs 3.27, 2.66, and 1.68 for 0-3, 4-7, and 8-10 min, respectively; reference >10 min). The pandemic period remained associated with lower 1-month survival after adjustment for BCPR initiation timing (aOR 0.86; 95% CI, 0.80-0.92).
CONCLUSIONS: Although the overall BCPR rate remained unchanged during the pandemic, time-to-event analysis identified a modest reduction in early BCPR initiation. Earlier BCPR was associated with better outcomes, but differences in its timing did not fully explain the lower survival during the pandemic.

title: Mechanical ventilation vs bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a randomized crossover noninferiority trial.
abstract:
AIM: Evidence guiding mechanical ventilation (MV) during CPR is limited, and device-calculated inspired tidal volume (VTi) during ongoing chest compressions may differ from the set volume during compressions. We compared VTi with protocolized MV and bag-valve ventilation (BVV) through an endotracheal tube for noninferiority.
METHODS: This single-center randomized crossover noninferiority trial enrolled 104 intubated adults meeting termination-of-resuscitation criteria without return of spontaneous circulation to receive BVV and MV in randomized order within a 5-min peri-termination window. Device-calculated VTi was recorded for 1 min per method during ongoing compressions. The primary outcome was the between-treatment difference in per-participant median VTi; the noninferiority margin was -150 mL (MV minus BVV).
RESULTS: Among 99 participants completing both periods, mean per-participant median VTi was 514.4 mL with BVV and 368.0 mL with MV; coefficients of variation were 40.1% and 28.3%. The adjusted mean difference was -146.2 mL (95% CI, -187.0 to -105.5). Because the lower bound crossed -150 mL, noninferiority was not demonstrated. Median VTi exceeded 10 mL/kg predicted body weight in 31.3% with BVV and 0% with MV, whereas values below 6 mL/kg occurred in 26.3% and 45.5%.
CONCLUSIONS: Protocolized MV produced lower and less variable device-calculated VTi than BVV but did not meet noninferiority. BVV had a wider upper tail, whereas MV more often produced values below 6 mL/kg. The unvalidated analyzer and absence of clinical outcomes limit interpretation.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Registry - India; CTRI/2024/08/072738.

title: Current European landscape of in-hospital cardiac arrest registries mapped by a cross-sectional survey including barriers and enablers setting up a registry.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) has a high mortality rate. To measure and improve resuscitation outcomes, data collection through registries plays a key role. This study aims to evaluate the current landscape of IHCA registries across national resuscitation councils affiliated with the European Resuscitation Council.
METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was distributed among national resuscitation councils collecting data on the presence and type of IHCA registries, registry coverage and data variables collected. Findings informed an expert discussion on barriers and enablers establishing such registries and potential next steps.
RESULTS: 30/34 (88%) national resuscitation councils replied to the survey. Seven have no IHCA registry (23%), 11 a local registry (37%), two a local and regional registry (7%), five a national registry (17%), and two countries participate in a national registry in another country (7%). Of the included registries 17 (94%) are collecting cardiac arrests in adults, 13 (72%) in children, and four (22%) in neonates. Most registries are collecting location of cardiac arrest (95%), the initial rhythm (95%), and if return of spontaneous circulation is achieved (100%), while long term neurological outcome is only collected by four registries (21%). Overall, the AI-assisted descriptive content analysis demonstrated broad consensus regarding the value of registries, while highlighting substantial logistical, legal, and financial barriers.
CONCLUSION: Our survey demonstrates considerable variation in the existence, population coverage, and data collection practices of IHCA registries. While core cardiac arrest variables are collected by most registries, data on long-term outcomes remain limited.

title: Changes in vital signs of hospitalized patients may not identify the need to escalate care as well as other bedside observations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Most Rapid Response Team activations rely on vital signs, frequently aggregated into weighted scoring systems, such as the National Early Warning Score (NEWS). Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of avoidable in-hospital deaths still result from delayed recognition of evolving pathophysiology and under-appreciation of patient or family concerns.
AIM: To compare the performance of NEWS with observations that can be rapidly assessed at the bedside without equipment or calculation, using death within 24 h as a surrogate marker for patients requiring immediate attention.
METHODS: Retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively on Rapid Response Team arrival to 4581 adult patients in general medical, surgical, or intermediate care units at a 450-bed regional medical center in California, USA.
RESULTS: Eight observations were identified that required no equipment to assess, which had a significant association with 24-h mortality; ranked by adjusted odds ratio these were (1) jaundice, (2) need for supplemental oxygen, (3) capillary refill time, (4) part or all of the body feeling cold, (5) objectively distressed breathing, (6) altered mentation, (7) dry skin, and (8) cyanosis. A logistic regression model of these 8 variables had a significantly higher discrimination for death within 24 h of Rapid Response Team arrival than NEWS (i.e., AUC of 0.790 SE 0.014 versus 0.707 SE 0.020, p < 0.0001).
CONCLUSION: In patients who trigger a Rapid Response Team call, bedside information that can be obtained rapidly without equipment or calculation, may provide earlier and more reliable signals of illness severity than NEWS and other early warning scores based on traditional vital signs.

title: Effect of orientation and contact area on foot chest compression quality: a simulation study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Concerns about fatigue and safety have prompted investigation of foot chest compressions as an alternative technique. To evaluate the effect of foot contact area heel vs ball-of-the-foot and foot orientation longitudinal vs transverse on the quality of foot chest compressions and physiological response in healthcare professionals.
METHODS: This 2 × 2 mixed-design simulation study examined heel and ball-of-the-foot techniques in longitudinal and transverse orientations over the sternum. Participants performed two consecutive two-minute sets of foot chest compressions on a Resusci Anne QCPR manikin. Compression quality parameters included depth, rate, recoil, and compression-to-release ratio. Heart rate was continuously monitored, energy expenditure was estimated using the Keytel equation, and perceived exertion was assessed using the Borg scale. Non-parametric statistical tests were applied with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: Eighty healthcare professionals completed the study. Mean compression depth ranged from 51 to 55 mm and the rate ranged from 118 to 123 compressions per minute across all conditions. The heel technique produced greater mean compression depth (54.2 ± 6.2 vs 51.6 ± 7.1 mm; p < 0.001), a higher percentage of compressions with adequate depth (81.8 ± 29.8% vs 72.7 ± 34.6%; p < 0.001), and a higher compression-to-release ratio (1.1 ± 0.3 vs 0.9 ± 0.2; p = 0.002) than the ball-of-the-foot technique. Compression rate, complete recoil, energy expenditure, heart rate, and perceived exertion were comparable between techniques. No significant differences were observed between longitudinal and transverse orientations.
CONCLUSIONS: Foot chest compressions achieved guideline-consistent depth and rate regardless of foot orientation. The heel technique produced greater mean depth and a higher percentage of adequate-depth compressions than the ball-of-the-foot technique. Physical demand was similar between techniques. These findings support the use of foot chest compressions as a feasible adjunct when hand compressions are not possible and justify further clinical evaluation.

title: Life satisfaction and self-rated health in long-term survivors after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR): associations with functional outcome, cognition, anxiety, depression, fatigue, and physical activity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The goal of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) is not only survival, but long-term satisfaction with life. Whether functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale; mRS), cognition, emotional symptoms, fatigue, and physical activity relate to life satisfaction in ECPR survivors remain unknown. We evaluated these aspects of health and their association with life satisfaction and self-rated health.
METHODS: This cross-sectional follow-up included survivors ≥1 year after ECPR at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden (2010-2021). Primary outcomes were life satisfaction (World Values Survey) and self-rated health (EQ-5D-5L VAS). Secondary outcomes were mRS, Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Mental Fatigue Scale (MFS), and self-reported physical activity. Exploratory multivariable linear regression assessed associations with primary outcomes.
RESULTS: Of 34 survivors, 26 (76.5%) participated; median follow-up was 5 [IQR 2-7] years; 96% had mRS 0-3. Median life satisfaction was 8 [6-9]/10 and self-rated health 81 [70-90]/100, similar to population reference values (7.55 and 80). Positive screen for cognitive impairment (MoCA < 26) was present in 56%, anxiety (HADS-A ≥ 8) 42%, depression (HADS-D ≥ 8) 15%, and fatigue (MFS ≥ 10.5) 50%. In exploratory multivariable analysis, moderate physical activity was associated with life satisfaction (B 0.36 per day/week; 95% CI 0.06-0.67; p = 0.023) and self-rated health (B 4.60; 0.71-8.50; p = 0.024).
CONCLUSION: Long-term ECPR survivors reported life satisfaction and self-rated health similar to population reference values. In exploratory multivariable analysis, moderate physical activity was the only variable associated with both. This supports assessing life satisfaction and physical activity in post-ECPR follow-up.

Video laryngoscopy versus direct laryngoscopy for pediatric emergency tracheal intubation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
AIM: To compare video laryngoscopy with direct laryngoscopy for pediatric intubation during cardiac arrest and peri-arrest scenarios.
METHODS: This systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420251081694) searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane from inception to May 1, 2026. Two authors independently screened studies; data were extracted by one and independently verified by a second reviewer. Eligible studies compared video versus direct laryngoscopy in pediatric acute care; emergency department, intensive care, and prehospital settings. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and RoB2. Critical outcomes were survival to hospital discharge, first-pass intubation success, overall intubation success, and severe tracheal intubation-associated events. Additional data included study design, setting, age, operator type, and device. Meta-analyses used random-effects Mantel-Haenszel models reporting risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies (17 observational, 1 RCT). First-pass success was higher with video laryngoscopy (72.2% vs 69.0%; RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.06-1.16; very low certainty). Severe adverse events were less frequent with video laryngoscopy (7.7% vs 11.8%; RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62-0.93; very low certainty). Overall success (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.01) and desaturation (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.01) were similar. No studies reported survival outcomes or data specific to cardiac arrest.
CONCLUSION: Among children undergoing emergency tracheal intubation, video laryngoscopy may be associated with improved first-pass success and fewer adverse events, although the certainty of evidence is very low and causal inferences are limited. No data were available for survival outcomes and cardiac arrest.
authors: International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation ILCOR Pediatric Life Support Task Force

title: Sex-based differences in clinical outcomes for non-prescription drug-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Non-prescription drug toxicity contributes to a substantial proportion of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs). Among OHCAs overall, previous reports have shown lower survival among females, compared to males. We examined sex-based differences in outcomes among non-prescription drug-associated OHCA (DA-OHCA).
METHODS: In this population-based observational cohort study using data from the BC Cardiac Arrest Registry (2019-24), we included emergency medical services (EMS)-treated OHCAs that had evidence of recent non-prescription drug use. The primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome, and secondary outcomes included survival at hospital discharge, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), and ROSC at emergency department (ED) arrival. We assessed the association between female sex (vs male) and outcomes using multivariable logistic regression models, adjusted for Utstein variables.
RESULTS: Among 47,051 EMS-Assessed OHCA, there were 4926 adult EMS-assessed DA-OHCA. We included 3133 adult EMS-treated DA-OHCAs, of whom 864 (28%) were female and 2269 (72%) were male, with a median age of 38 (interquartile range [IQR] 30-49) and 40 (IQR 32-52) years, respectively. Favorable neurological outcomes occurred in 108 (13%) females and 212 (9.6%) males. Female sex was not associated with favorable neurological outcome (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.32, 95% CI 0.97, 1.79), prehospital ROSC (aOR 1.00, 95% CI 0.83, 1.19), or ROSC at ED arrival (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84, 1.22), but was associated with an increased odds survival to hospital discharge (aOR 1.34; 95% CI 1.01, 1.77).
CONCLUSIONS: Among DA-OHCA, female sex was not independently associated with favorable neurological outcomes, but was associated with a higher odds of survival to hospital discharge.

title: Is Ohio's high school CPR requirement reaching students? A survey of central Ohio high school students.
Assessing Swedish guidelines for prehospital bleeding control: a cross-sectional appraisal using AGREE II.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-quality clinical practice guidelines are essential for safe and consistent prehospital bleeding control, particularly in settings with variable geography and transport times. This study appraised the methodological quality of Swedish regional prehospital guidelines for traumatic external haemorrhage using the AGREE II instrument.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included clinical practice guidelines requested from all 21 Swedish healthcare regions. Guideline quality was assessed independently by two appraisers using AGREE II, which evaluates 23 items across six domains. Domain scores were calculated as percentages of the maximum possible score.
RESULTS: Complete responses were obtained from 15 of 21 regions. Overall methodological quality was low across the included guidelines. The highest median domain score was observed for clarity of presentation, whereas rigour of development, stakeholder involvement, applicability, and editorial independence scored poorly. Most guidelines lacked explicit descriptions of evidence search strategies, criteria for selecting evidence, links between recommendations and supporting evidence, update procedures, and declarations of editorial independence.
CONCLUSIONS: Swedish regional prehospital guidelines for traumatic external bleeding control showed limited methodological quality when assessed using AGREE II. Future guideline development should prioritise transparent evidence linkage, multidisciplinary stakeholder involvement, clear implementation considerations, scheduled updating, and adaptation to regional differences in transport and evacuation times.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

title: Discussing lung cancer management options in the emergency department.
Prevalence of Persistent Severe Hypertension and Rates of Treatment Among Pregnant Patients in the Prehospital Setting.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) contribute to maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality and require time-sensitive intervention. In April 2025, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), in collaboration with the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP) and the National Association of EMTs (NAEMT), published new guidelines on the prehospital management of elevated blood pressure in pregnancy. The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of persistent severe hypertension among pregnant patients encountered by prehospital clinicians, characterize baseline frequency of pre-guideline treatment, and establish a benchmark to inform implementation of these guidelines.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study using the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative public release research dataset (January 1 to December 31, 2024). We identified all 9-1-1 ground EMS scene responses for patients documented as pregnant beyond 20 weeks of gestation. We excluded injury-related encounters and patients outside the World Health Organization-defined childbearing age range (15 to 49 years). Consistent with the new guidelines, we defined persistent severe hypertension as at least two documented blood pressure measurements with systolic blood pressure ≥ 160 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mmHg. We defined guideline-adherent treatment as administration of both magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) and an antihypertensive medication (labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine).
RESULTS: We identified 39,546 eligible 9-1-1 ground EMS scene responses for patients beyond 20 weeks of gestation. The prevalence of persistent severe hypertension was 3.1% (n = 1,234/39,546). Among these patients, 77 (6.2%) received magnesium sulfate only, 19 (1.5%) received an antihypertensive medication only, and 10 (0.8%) received guideline-adherent treatment with both magnesium sulfate and an antihypertensive medication.
CONCLUSIONS: Approximately 1 in 32 pregnant patients beyond 20 weeks of gestation encountered by prehospital clinicians had persistent severe hypertension. In the year prior to dissemination of the 2025 ACOG, NAEMSP, and NAEMT-supported guidelines, fewer than 1% received guideline-adherent treatment with both magnesium sulfate and an antihypertensive medication. These findings establish a national benchmark and identify opportunities to improve prehospital care through protocol development, medication availability, clinician education, and implementation of updated guidelines.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted, Electrocardiogram-Derived, Sequential Rule-Based Decision Tree for Exclusion of Acute Coronary Syndrome as the Etiology of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: After out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), deciding which patients without ST-segment elevation warrant emergency coronary angiography is difficult, as standard electrocardiogram (ECG), troponin, and echocardiography are limited in the early post-arrest window. We aimed to develop a sequential rule-based decision tree to identify post-ROSC patients in whom acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is unlikely to be the arrest etiology.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective study, adult patients with OHCA were divided into development (2020-2024; n=329) and temporal validation (2025; n=71) cohorts. Post-ROSC 12-lead ECGs were analyzed by a deep-learning platform generating ten digital biomarkers. Five candidate biomarkers were combined into a rhythm-stratified sequential decision tree under a zero false-negative constraint; its performance was compared with that of individual biomarkers and validated in the temporal cohort.
RESULTS: The tree classified 171/329 (52.0%) and 32/71 (45.1%) patients in the development and validation cohorts, respectively, as "ACS not likely," with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified at any node. Yield concentrated in the non-shockable subgroup, in which the model excluded 169/261 (64.8%) non-ACS cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC], 0.824), outperforming each individual biomarker. In the shockable subgroup, which carries a high pretest probability of ACS, 38/40 patients (95.0%) were retained as "ACS not excluded."
CONCLUSIONS: A rhythm-stratified, rule-based decision tree combining AI-assisted ECG-derived biomarkers classified approximately half of post-OHCA patients as "ACS not likely" with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified, principally in the non-shockable subgroup. This transparent, bedside-deployable framework warrants prospective multicenter evaluation.

title: Ventilation Monitoring in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Care.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Adherence to American Heart Association (AHA) ventilation guidelines during cardiac arrest is challenging.
METHODS: Prospective, Before/After quality assurance study determining adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by Milwaukee County Emergency Medical Services and Kenosha Fire in Wisconsin using (Before) end tidal carbon dioxide [ETCO2] to monitor ventilations - Real BVM Help® applied but blinded versus (After) Real BVM Help®.
PRIMARY ENDPOINTS: mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in-target for rate, tidal volume, and both rate and tidal volume. AHA 2020 guidelines were followed.
RESULTS: From 9/29/22-12/22/23, 278 patients were entered (148 Before/130 After). Average age: 62.3±16.7 years; 185 (67%) male. Mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in Before/After Groups in-target for rate (47.7±25.1% vs 74.4±24.1% respectively, p<0.0001), tidal volume (15.3±15.4% vs 45.4±23.8% respectively, p<0.0001), and rate and tidal volume (7.5±9.6% vs 39.0±23.3% respectively, p<0.0001) were significantly higher in the After Group. In the Before Group, using ETCO2 to monitor all ventilations (N=22,037 ventilations), only 43.8% were in-target for rate, 13.5% in-target for tidal volume, and 6.8% in-target for rate and tidal volume with a lower-than-target tidal volume delivered in 58.2% of all ventilations.
CONCLUSION: Real BVM Help® was associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines. ETCO2 monitoring failed to approach both rate and tidal volume guideline adherence with a lower-than-target tidal volume being the most common parameter delivered out-of-target (58.2%). Ventilation rate and tidal volume monitoring with real-time feedback should be considered during treatment of cardiac arrest.

title: Early Identification of Recurrent Out-of-hospital Cardiac Arrest Using Clinical ECG Features.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) after initial return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is associated with relatively poor outcomes. Early identification of rearrest might allow for intervention to prevent rearrest. In this study, we sought to determine whether clinical ECG features can predict rearrest.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients who achieved ROSC between 2018-2024. We evaluated the association of ECG features (QRS width, standard deviation of NN intervals, root mean square of successive NN interval differences, and percentage of NN intervals that differ by more than 50 milliseconds) within individual 15-second segments throughout a 5-minute window prior to rearrest as well as their temporal trends over the 5-minute analytic window.
RESULTS: Of the 1,489 OHCA patients achieving ROSC, 1,298 were analyzed; 528 (40.7%) experienced rearrest. Rearrest patients were older, less likely to receive bystander CPR (48.7% vs. 61.9%), and had lower survival (20.4% vs. 43.1%) and favorable neurologic outcomes (7.8% vs. 21.2%; all p<0.001). We found lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher HR variability in those with rearrest. Identification was highest 1 minute prior to rearrest (AUROC 0.74), declining beyond 3 minutes. Models using temporal trends achieved AUROC 0.67; strongest predictors were heart rate variability measures and QRS width.
CONCLUSION: Established ECG features achieved good prediction for rearrest with identification improving closer to time of rearrest. Future work leveraging novel features or more advanced artificial intelligence models may further improve prediction.

title: Severity and resource utilisation among trauma patients undergoing trauma team activation in four Danish trauma units: a prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evidence on trauma epidemiology and outcomes largely originates from major trauma centres, while data from regional trauma units remain limited. The aim of this study was to describe the epidemiology, management, and outcomes of patients undergoing trauma team activation in the trauma units of Region Zealand, Denmark.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective multicentre observational study across four regional trauma units in Region Zealand, Denmark, between 1 March 2024 and 28 February 2025. All consecutive patients undergoing trauma team activation were included. Data included demographics, injury mechanisms, injury severity, in-hospital management, and mortality. Analyses were descriptive.
RESULTS: A total of 1611 patients were included. Median age was 38 years [IQR 20-58], and 60.5% were male. The most common injury mechanisms were traffic-related injuries (53%), falls (22%), and equestrian-related accidents (13%). Median Injury Severity Score was 1 [IQR 0-5] and 94% had Injury Severity Score < 16. Secondary transfer to a major trauma centre occurred in 3.8% of cases, and 90-day mortality was 2.6%. Trauma admissions occurred predominantly outside regular daytime workflow, with a peak in the late afternoon and early evening. Median TTA duration was 58 minutes [IQR 43-76] and CT imaging was performed in 86.7% of cases. Following trauma team activation, 55.2% of patients were discharged directly and 4.6% required intensive care unit admission.
CONCLUSIONS: Most patients undergoing trauma team activation in regional trauma units had minor injuries, were discharged directly from the emergency department, and infrequently required intensive care unit admission or secondary transfer. Despite this, trauma team activation had a median duration around one hour and showed marked diurnal variation, with a peak in the late afternoon and early evening when staffing and clinical resources are typically more limited. These findings highlight opportunities to optimise trauma team activation criteria and organisational structures to better align resource utilisation with patient acuity.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.
METHODS: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

title: Documented Thermoregulation Strategies Alone Do Not Benefit Comatose In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivors.
Tracheal Intubation-Associated Cardiac Arrest in Critically Ill Children: The Medical Equivalent of a 100-Year Flood.

Variation in Pediatric Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Development and Validation of a Survival Model for Risk-Standardized Survival Rates: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To develop and internally validate a multivariable prediction model for survival to hospital discharge after pediatric extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), and to use this model to derive risk-standardized survival rates (RSSRs) and quantify between-hospital variation in outcomes.
DESIGN: Retrospective multicenter cohort study.
SETTING: Hospitals contributing to the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry between 2020 and 2023.
PATIENTS: Children (< 18 yr) treated with ECPR for IHCA.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Eligible patients were identified from the ELSO Registry and split into derivation (N = 1060) and validation (N = 317) cohorts using a hospital-stratified split to preserve within-hospital clustering. Survival prediction models were derived using penalized logistic regression with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. A full-event model incorporating 14 routinely available clinical variables demonstrated fair discrimination (area under the curve, 0.728 in the derivation cohort and 0.678 in the validation cohort) and good calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, 0.995; Brier score, 0.222 in the validation cohort). This model was embedded in a multilevel logistic regression model to generate hospital-level RSSRs for centers reporting five or more ECPR cases. Between-hospital variation was quantified using the median odds ratio, which was 1.30 (95% CI, 1.11-1.93), indicating significant differences in survival likelihood between centers after adjusting for patient-level risk.
CONCLUSIONS: In a large, international cohort of pediatric ECPR patients, we developed and internally validated a clinically interpretable model for survival to hospital discharge. The model performance as a discriminator likely limits its use as a standalone tool for clinical decision-making. However, strong internal calibration allowed for determination of hospital-level RSSRs, which revealed significant inter-hospital variability. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of developing a risk-adjustment model capable of estimating hospital-level RSSRs. Additional external validation and evaluation of residual case-mix differences are needed before such models can be used for benchmarking across pediatric ECPR centers.

title: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients.
abstract: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a lifesaving strategy for refractory cardiac arrest, restoring systemic perfusion when conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation fails. However, ECPR profoundly disrupts haemostasis, driven by the combined effects of whole-body ischaemia-reperfusion injury, systemic inflammation, endothelial activation, platelet dysfunction, and blood contact with extracorporeal surfaces. Together, these processes create a highly dynamic and unstable thromboinflammatory milieu, marked by the simultaneous risk of thrombosis and life-threatening bleeding. Systemic anticoagulation is required to maintain circuit patency and prevent thromboembolic complications, yet optimal strategies remain uncertain. Haemostasis during ECPR is highly dynamic, shaped by the underlying aetiology of cardiac arrest, patient-specific characteristics, and circuit-related factors. This complexity underscores the limitations of fixed anticoagulation targets and the need for individualized, context-sensitive management guided by continuous clinical and laboratory assessment. Despite the increasing global adoption of ECPR, high-quality evidence to guide anticoagulation practices remains scarce. Current strategies are largely extrapolated from other extracorporeal life support populations, contributing to substantial inter-centre variability. This review synthesizes the available evidence on coagulopathy and anticoagulation in adult patients receiving ECPR and discusses emerging approaches to monitoring and anticoagulation management.

title: Development of a quality metric to measure bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation in out of hospital cardiac arrest: A modified Delphi study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains a significant global public health challenge, with survival heavily dependent on early and high-quality bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Current data collection frameworks lack standardised tools to assess the quality of bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to develop a preliminary consensus-based quality metric for use in both research and clinical practice.
SETTING: This study was conducted in the United Kingdom with international representation within the Delphi panel.
PARTICIPANTS: A total of 104 participants registered, with 62, 48, and 18 completing rounds one to three, respectively in the Delphi panel. The panel consisted of Doctors, advanced practitioners, Paramedics, Nurses and academics.
METHODS: A modified Delphi method was employed to identify and define quality indicators. Criteria were developed from a literature review, stakeholder input, and panel consensus. A diverse expert panel, including clinicians, researchers, educators, and informed laypersons, participated in three iterative rounds (two online surveys and a final virtual consensus meeting). Consensus was defined as ≥75% agreement on a 1-5 Likert scale.
RESULTS: Eleven criteria achieved consensus for inclusion, encompassing core mechanical parameters (e.g., chest compression rate, depth, recoil) and contextual factors (e.g., dispatcher instruction, time from recognition to emergency call, and automated external defibrillator use). All criteria were agreed to be scored dichotomously. Two composite indicators were created to streamline overlapping elements.
CONCLUSION: The provisional metric reflects both established guidelines and evolving evidence on factors influencing bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation effectiveness. The inclusion of time and system-based criteria acknowledges the broader context in which cardiopulmonary resuscitation is delivered. Once validated in future studies this metric has potential for practical relevance for feedback tools, service evaluation, and research standardisation. This study was not registered.
journal_full: International journal of nursing studies advances

title: Response to: "Moving the dial on out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survival in Aotearoa New Zealand".
Efficiency of Rescue Paramedic Hoist versus Underslung Antenna in Helicopter-Based Avalanche Searches: A Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Survival for avalanche victims is time-dependent, and survival is often reliant on ground companion rescue. Due to the time-critical nature of burial, remote locations, and high frequency of concomitant severe trauma, helicopters are often dispatched to these incidents. While helicopter-based transceiver searches are standard, the most efficient deployment strategy, either using an underslung antenna or hoisting a rescue paramedic (RP) with a handheld transceiver, remains unknown. This study compared the operational efficiency of these two methods in the Norwegian Search-and-Rescue (SAR) Helicopter Service.
METHODS: A dual randomized, experimental field trial was conducted with the on-duty SAR helicopter and crew at the Ørland Main Airforce Base (Trøndelag, Norway). A simulated avalanche area of 80 × 150 meters was used, and six avalanche transceivers were buried at approximately 0.5m depth across the area. Only one transceiver was active at each run, and the locations were randomized to prevent crew memorization. The sequence of which procedure to use was also randomized. Four operational timestamps were recorded: First Signal, Optimal Signal, RP on Ground, and Transceiver Found.
RESULTS: Over three days, a total of 25 trial runs were performed, 13 with Antenna Search and 12 with RP Hoist Search. The RP Hoist Search was significantly faster in both time to Optimal Signal, with a difference between the groups of 29 seconds (95% CI, 9 - 50), and time for RP on Ground, with a difference between the groups of 124 seconds (95% CI, 98 - 151). For the total time to Transceiver Found, the difference between the groups was 143 seconds (95% CI, 113 - 172; P <0.001). Furthermore, the RP Hoist Search resulted in significantly faster fine search on the ground.
CONCLUSION: This randomized, experimental field trial comparing two currently used standard search procedures in the Norwegian SAR service showed that the RP Hoist Search was significantly more efficient than the Antenna Search for localizing buried avalanche victims, reducing total localization time by more than two minutes. Given that survival probability is reduced after 10-15 minutes of burial, this time saving may be clinically significant. The findings support that RP Hoist Search is an effective localization strategy for SAR helicopter services with comparable hoist systems.

title: Early post-resuscitation profiles after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A latent class analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early cardiopulmonary heterogeneity after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) may be associated with prognosis and treatment response.
OBJECTIVES: To identify early post-resuscitation profiles and explore their associations with outcomes and randomized treatment effects.
METHODS: In this post hoc analysis of the BOX pulmonary artery catheter substudy, latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to early clinical, echocardiographic, and invasive hemodynamic variables. The primary outcome was 365-day all-cause mortality. Exploratory cross-cohort replication used a separately fitted LCA in the Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) cohort, with 180-day mortality.
RESULTS: Among 700 BOX patients, a two-class model was selected. Class 2 (n = 352) showed longer time to return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), higher lactate, greater cardiopulmonary dysfunction, higher filling pressures, and greater noradrenaline requirements. Mortality was 48% in Class 2 versus 21% in Class 1. No treatment interaction was detected for mean arterial pressure (MAP; P = 0.606), oxygenation (P = 0.483), or fever-control duration (P = 0.946). Mortality discrimination was not superior to time to ROSC alone. In 152 TTM patients, mortality was 38% versus 24% (P = 0.057), with less pronounced hemodynamic separation.
CONCLUSION: Two early post-resuscitation profiles were identified after OHCA, with more pronounced separation in filling pressures than cardiac output in BOX. The profiles were associated with prognosis but did not identify differential responses to the randomized interventions.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: BOX trial, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03141099; TTM trial, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT01020916.
journal_full: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

title: Spatial accessibility and equity of emergency medical services: Evidence from Ningbo.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Timely access to emergency medical services (EMS) is essential for improving survival outcomes and public health. In rapidly urbanizing Chinese cities, disparities in EMS accessibility are increasingly shaped by the spatial distribution of hospitals, population concentration, transport infrastructure, and built environment conditions. However, relatively few studies have simultaneously compared emergency and non-emergency medical accessibility and examined their spatial equity and influencing factors in medium-sized coastal cities. This study evaluates the spatial accessibility, equity, and clustering characteristics of EMS in Ningbo, China, and identifies the key built environment factors influencing these patterns.
METHODS: The shortest travel time model, based on API data, was employed to measure EMS accessibility for both emergency (ambulance) and non-emergency (public transport) scenarios across five core urban districts of Ningbo. The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient were applied to assess healthcare equity. We used global Moran's I and local indicators of spatial association (LISA) to explore spatial clustering and a multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) model to analyze spatial heterogeneity in influencing factors across built environment dimensions.
RESULTS: Both emergency and non-emergency medical services exhibited significant spatial disparities, decreasing gradually from the city center toward the periphery. The Gini coefficients for emergency and non-emergency models were 0.5156 and 0.4898, respectively, indicating substantial inequity. Strong spatial clustering was observed (global Moran's I = 0.846, p < 0.01), with high-value clusters concentrated in central districts and low-value clusters in mountainous outskirts. MGWR results revealed that accessibility was positively affected by the number of bus stops, road density, bus route density, and distance to the Central Business District (CBD), but negatively impacted by building density and development intensity. The MGWR model's explanatory power (R2 = 0.584) demonstrated significant spatial heterogeneity in these relationships. Building density and bus route density exerted the strongest local effects among the eleven built environment indicators.
CONCLUSION: EMS accessibility in Ningbo exhibits evident spatial inequality and clustering characteristics. Peripheral and mountainous areas remain disadvantaged, especially under non-emergency public transport conditions. Improving road connectivity, expanding public transit coverage, optimizing hospital and EMS resource allocation, and strengthening services in underserved areas can help reduce healthcare accessibility inequities. These findings provide an empirical foundation for optimizing EMS resource allocation for urban policymakers as well as offer practical insights for other rapidly urbanizing cities facing similar challenges.

title: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty in Paramedic Students: A START Triage Perspective.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study examined whether intolerance of uncertainty and decision-making styles were associated with theoretical START triage knowledge among paramedic students. Secondary exploratory analyses assessed psychosocial differences according to self-rated decision-making under stress, perceived coping with uncertainty, professional motivation, and challenges in prehospital emergency care.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 121 students from a First and Emergency Aid Program completed a self-administered paper-based questionnaire including a sociodemographic form, the Decision-Making Styles Scale, the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-12, and the START Triage Knowledge Test. Data were collected in classroom settings under researcher supervision between May and June 2025 and analyzed using descriptive statistics, group comparisons, and correlation analyses.
RESULTS: The mean theoretical START triage knowledge score was 69.99 ± 14.76. START knowledge was not significantly associated with intolerance of uncertainty or decision-making style subscale scores. Exploratory analyses identified associations between psychosocial scores and self-rated decision-making under stress, coping with uncertainty, professional motivation, and perceived challenges.
CONCLUSIONS: Theoretical START triage knowledge was not associated with intolerance of uncertainty or decision-making styles. Secondary findings were limited to self-reported psychosocial associations. The study assessed declarative knowledge and did not evaluate START application in simulated or field settings. Future studies should use simulation-based, scenario-based, or observational outcomes.
journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

title: Association between mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
abstract:
AIM: The effect of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) during intermittent positive pressure ventilation in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on outcome is unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between the use of PEEP during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and clinical outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients.
METHODS: We conducted a single-centre observational cohort study using a retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively within a dedicated research registry of adult OHCA patients managed by a physician-staffed prehospital emergency medical team. All included patients were intubated and ventilated either with mechanical ventilation using PEEP or with manual ventilation without PEEP. Intratracheal pressure was continuously recorded via a catheter connected to a portable device, allowing objective verification of PEEP application and ventilation rate. The association between mechanical ventilation with PEEP use and clinical outcomes was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for relevant confounders.
RESULTS: 362 patients were included, with a median age of 65 years (54-79), of whom 250 (69.1%) were male. Median ventilation rate was 15 breaths/min (10-19). Of all patients, 149 (41.2%) achieved Return Of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) and 31 (8.6%) survived to hospital discharge. The adjusted odds ratio (OR) of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for achieving ROSC was 1.58 (95% CI 1.01-2.50, p = 0.048). The unadjusted OR of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for survival to hospital discharge was 2.22 (95% CI 1.03-4.78; p = 0.037).
CONCLUSION: The use of mechanical ventilation with PEEP during CPR in OHCA patients was associated with higher likelihood of ROSC.
journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine

title: Layperson naloxone administration and subsequent emergency medical services care for opioid overdose.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Layperson-administered naloxone is increasingly common before emergency medical services (EMS) arrival. However, EMS care following naloxone administered by laypeople rather than trained responders remains poorly characterized.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study used the 2023 National EMS Information System dataset and included 9-1-1 activations for individuals aged ≥ 16 years with an EMS impression of opioid overdose and documented naloxone administration before EMS arrival. Exposures were layperson-administered naloxone (LAN) or trained responder-administered naloxone (TRAN; e.g., police, firefighter). The primary outcome was subsequent EMS naloxone administration. Secondary outcomes included total number of EMS naloxone administrations, advanced airway intervention, cardiac arrest, and EMS transport. We used descriptive statistics, t-tests, and multivariable logistic regression estimating adjusted odds ratios (aOR).
RESULTS: Among 26,087 EMS activations, 8016 (30.7%) received LAN and 18,071 (69.3%) TRAN. Any subsequent EMS naloxone administration was less frequent following LAN (24.4% vs. 34.8%; P < .001); when EMS did administer additional naloxone, the mean number of administrations was slightly higher following LAN (mean difference 0.05, 95%CI 0.02-0.09; P = .001). Advanced airway attempts (1.6% vs. 1.4%, P = .160) and cardiac arrest (6.6% vs. 6.0%, P = .080) were uncommon. EMS transport occurred less often after LAN (79.4% vs. 84.4%, P < .001). In adjusted analyses, LAN was associated with lower odds of subsequent EMS naloxone administration (aOR 0.73; 95%CI 0.68-0.78) and EMS transport (aOR 0.78; 95%CI 0.73-0.84).
CONCLUSIONS: Layperson-administered naloxone was associated with less frequent EMS naloxone administration and lower rates of EMS transport. These findings support layperson overdose response while highlighting the need to better understand post-overdose care trajectories.

title: Heat Stroke Cooling Devices for Prehospital Use: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Heat stroke and heat exhaustion (HS/HE) are life-threatening conditions requiring immediate intervention. Cooling devices play a critical role in emergency and prehospital care, yet their effectiveness and field readiness are inconsistently reported. This systematic review evaluates commercially available cooling devices for the treatment of HS/HE with an emphasis on device feasibility, performance, and suitability for prehospital and remote deployment.
METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in August/October 2025 across academic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Compendex, Engineering Village, and IEEE Xplore) and gray literature via Google Advanced Search. Academic records were screened using Rayyan, while gray literature was organized in Excel with the aid of a custom HTML scraper. Devices were included if they met the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) definition of a medical device, were designed for adult human use, and specifically addressed HS/HE. Parameters extracted included working principle, cooling rate, weight, dimensions, volume, power requirements, external resource demands, and reusability. Cooling performance was benchmarked using thresholds reported by McDermott, et al, and portability was assessed using the MIL-STD-1472H single-person carriage limit of ≤16kg.
RESULTS: A total of 18 devices were identified and evaluated. Only three met the ideal cooling rate threshold (≥0.155°C/minute), and two others achieved acceptable performance (0.078-0.154°C/minute). Approximately 61% of devices did not report cooling rate data. Five devices met field portability criteria (≤16kg), though most were limited by reliance on water, power, or disposable components. Only one device demonstrated feasibility for remote use; this device, however, lacked full reusability.
CONCLUSIONS: No device meets the combined criteria of effectiveness, portability, field readiness, and reusability for HS/HE treatment. Current FDA pathways do not require reporting of key performance metrics, highlighting a regulatory gap. There is a need for development of field-appropriate solutions and revised evaluation standards that prioritize cooling performance, resource independence, and usability in austere environments.

title: Timing of the Adrenaline Administration in Witnessed Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Retrospective, National Cohort Study in Japan, Using a 2014-2020 Dataset.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: We evaluated the association between the timing of initial adrenaline administration and outcomes in witnessed pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA).
DESIGN: A multicenter, retrospective cohort study addressing resuscitation time bias by performing a risk-set matching analysis using time-dependent propensity scores.
SETTING: Analysis of data from the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine OHCA (JAAM-OHCA) registry, which is a nationwide, multicenter, prospective collection of prehospital and in-hospital data involving Japanese patients with OHCA.
PATIENTS: Pediatric patients (< 18 yr) with witnessed OHCA who received adrenaline, during the period June 2014 to December 2020.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We compared patients who received adrenaline in specific time intervals (1-10, 11-15, 16-20, 21-25, or 26-30 min) after first contact with emergency medical services with those who still had not received adrenaline during the same time. The primary and secondary outcomes were survival and favorable neurologic outcome at one month, defined as a Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category score of 1-3. We identified a total of 259 OHCA patients who had received adrenaline at 1-10, 11-15, 16-20, 21-25, 26-30, and 31 minutes or later; at each respective time point, there were 15, 39, 62, 55, 37, and 51 patients. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs for 1-month survival at each time group compared with patients at risk were: 1-10 minutes, RR, 2.94 (95% CI, 0.38-22.81); 11-15 minutes, RR, 0.97 (95% CI, 0.30-3.12); 16-20 minutes, RR, 1.00 (95% CI, 0.29-3.48); 21-25 minutes, RR, 1.35 (95% CI, 0.54-3.40); and 26-30 minutes, RR, 1.71 (95% CI, 0.27-10.78). We failed to identify an association between time interval and greater or lesser probability of survival or neurologic outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: In the JAAM-OHCA registry, with pediatric data from 2014 to 2020, we failed to identify an association between earlier adrenaline administration and greater probability of 1-month survival or favorable neurologic outcomes.
journal_full: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies

title: Mapping the research landscape of UAV- and eVTOL-enabled emergency medical services: a bibliometric analysis, scoping review, and policy tool assessment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly recognized as transformative technologies for emergency medical services (EMS). Despite a growing body of evidence on drone-delivered automated external defibrillators (AEDs), blood product logistics, and eVTOL air ambulance simulations, no study has comprehensively mapped this interdisciplinary research landscape while simultaneously analyzing the policy frameworks that govern its implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a triple-method study integrating bibliometric analysis, a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and quantitative policy text analysis. Bibliometric mapping covered 2015 to 2026. The scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology with the PAGER (Patterns, Advances, Gaps, Evidence, Recommendations) synthesis framework, including 168 studies. Policy analysis applied the Rothwell and Zegveld policy tool classification and the Policy Modeling Consistency (PMC) Index to 62 Chinese policy documents related to low-altitude economy and emergency medical rescue (2020-2025), yielding 526 codable policy provisions.
RESULTS: The bibliometric analysis identified 683 publications across five thematic clusters, with exponential growth from 2022 onward. The scoping review of 168 studies synthesized evidence showing drone-delivered AEDs arrived before ambulances in 67% of cases (median lead time 3 min 14 s), blood product drone delivery reduced transport time by 61%, and eVTOL air ambulance simulations halved advanced life support response times. All 964 modeled drone networks were cost-effective under model assumptions, improving OHCA survival by 21%-46%. Policy analysis of 62 Chinese documents revealed structural imbalance: supply-side and environmental tools constituted 75.3% of provisions while demand-side tools accounted for only 24.7%. The mean PMC Index was 7.46 (SD = 0.89), with timeliness (0.73) and policy measures (0.72) as the weakest dimensions.
CONCLUSION: The evidence base for UAV/eVTOL-enabled emergency medical services is approaching the consistency needed to inform health systems planning, although no formal risk-of-bias appraisal was undertaken, and a critical disconnect persists between technological readiness and policy infrastructure. We propose a "dual-wheel drive, four-chain integration" framework encompassing scenario implementation and ecosystem cultivation across infrastructure, industrial innovation, institutional policy, and human capital dimensions. This framework offers a roadmap for translating fragmented pilot programs into sustainable, equity-enhancing emergency medical service systems.

title: Paramedic attitudinal profiles regarding pediatric pain management: A latent class analysis in a standardized emergency medical services system.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Pediatric pain is frequently under-recognized and undertreated in prehospital emergency care despite guideline-based recommendations, and practice variation may persist even within standardized emergency medical services (EMS) systems.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional survey of paramedics working in a nationally standardized EMS system in Türkiye to identify latent attitudinal (self-reported) profiles related to pediatric prehospital analgesia and to examine whether profile membership differed by demographic or professional characteristics. Attitudinal items underwent exploratory dimensionality assessment and were then modeled using latent class analysis.
RESULTS: Among 129 paramedics, two profiles were identified: proactive/system-oriented (57.4%) and conservative/low-engagement (42.6%). The proactive/system-oriented profile reported higher endorsement of decision-support tools (mobile drug-dosing applications and in-ambulance analgesia algorithms), more consistent self-reported post-analgesia vital sign monitoring, and greater self-reported use of non-pharmacologic adjuncts. The conservative/low-engagement profile reported lower intended engagement with these self-reported practices and greater reliance on perceived barriers. Profile membership was not associated with age, sex, years of EMS experience, or prior training.
CONCLUSİON: Distinct attitudinal (self-reported) profiles regarding pediatric prehospital analgesia were identified; whether these profiles translate into objectively observed analgesia delivery requires validation using routine documentation and, where feasible, linked ED outcomes.

title: Heat stroke during the 2025 summer heatwave in Northwestern India: A tertiary care emergency department case series.
abstract: Heat stroke is a life-threatening medical emergency, characterized by a core body temperature above 40°C with central nervous system dysfunction. Population living in arid and northwestern regions are particularly vulnerable during prolonged summer heatwaves. This case series describes the clinical spectrum and outcomes of patients with heat stroke presenting to the emergency department of a tertiary care teaching hospital in such a region during the 2025 heatwaves. We retrospectively reviewed 10 consecutive patients with heat stroke admitted between May 1, 2025 and July 31, 2025. Data on demographics, clinical presentation, cooling methods, laboratory parameters, complications, and outcomes were extracted from the medical records. Ten patients (7 male and 3 female) ranged in age from 22 to 78 years; six had classic (nonexertional) heat stroke; and four had exertional heat stroke (EHS). All presented with hyperthermia (mean 41.2°C) and altered mental status, ranging from agitation to coma. The complications were frequent: acute kidney injury occurred in 70% of patients, severe rhabdomyolysis (creatine phosphokinase >10,000 U/L) in 40% (all EHS), hepatic dysfunction in 80%, and disseminated intravascular coagulation in 20%. Rapid, active cooling was initiated in all cases. The overall in-hospital mortality was 20%. This series highlights the severe, multisystem nature of heat stroke in this setting and underlines the importance of early recognition, prompt cooling, and aggressive supportive care.

title: Development and Initial Assessment of a Low-Cost Skin Tear Management Task Trainer for Paramedic Education.
abstract: Inappropriate management of skin tears can result in pain, delayed healing, infection, and reduced mobility. There is growing interest in expanding the paramedic scope of practice to include skin tear management. However, a lack of scalable, low-cost task trainers poses barriers to the implementation of structured training initiatives. Hence, this technical report describes the development of a scalable, low-cost skin tear management task trainer for paramedic education using digital technologies and additive manufacturing, and provides an initial assessment of its perceived acceptability. Three skin tear management task trainer prototypes (type 1, no skin loss; type 2, partial skin loss; type 3, complete skin loss) were co-developed by a team of researchers and an advanced care paramedic. The development process consisted of two iterative rounds of prototyping, testing, and refinement, after which 14 type 1 task trainers were fabricated, integrated into a paramedic training initiative, and assessed across three domains, including (1) self-efficacy, (2) realism, and (3) educational value. Quantitative and qualitative data were collected and analyzed. Approximate fabrication time per unit was 20-30 minutes of active labor and 80-90 minutes of curing, depending on the skin tear type. The total cost of the materials used to fabricate the task trainer was 35.29 Canadian dollars (including taxes). This amount excludes capital equipment, including the three-dimensional printer, computer-aided design and slicing software, and reusable molds and templates, which are amortized across multiple task trainers. Participants rated the task trainer highly for perceived self-efficacy (4.68/5), realism (4.64/5), and educational value (4.85/5). These scores reflect participants' perceptions rather than objective measures of skill acquisition. Qualitative data yielded three descriptive categories: (1) visual and tactile realism, (2) pathological realism, and (3) procedural complexity and adaptability. Overall, both quantitative and qualitative data indicated that participants perceived the task trainer as an acceptable training tool. This technical report demonstrates the feasibility of developing a scalable, low-cost skin tear management task trainer using digital technologies and additive manufacturing. Future work will focus on standardizing skin flap thickness and developing task trainers with varying skin tear shapes and sizes, anatomical locations, wound presentations, and levels of procedural complexity. Next steps involve implementing the task trainer broadly across paramedic training initiatives and formally evaluating its impact on procedural skill acquisition and maintenance, confidence, and decision-making abilities.
